lessonTitle: Dose-Response Relationships: Potency, Efficacy, EC50 and the Logarithmic Axis

blocks.text: Two diuretics are compared in a trial. One produces a given urine output at a tenth of the dose of the other, yet the second can, at higher doses, produce a far larger maximum urine output. Which is the better drug? The honest answer depends on whether you are asking about dose or about maximal effect, and these are separate properties.

blocks.markdown: A **graded dose-response relationship** describes how the size of a response in one system (for example fall in blood pressure, in mmHg) changes as the dose or concentration of a drug rises. Plotted against concentration, the curve is a rectangular hyperbola that rises and then flattens as receptors become saturated. Two features characterise it: where it sits along the dose axis (**potency**) and how high it climbs (**efficacy**).

blocks.title: Potency, efficacy and EC50
blocks.text: EC50 is the concentration of a drug that produces 50% of its own maximal response. Potency is the amount of drug needed for a given effect; a lower EC50 means higher potency. Efficacy (maximal efficacy, Emax) is the greatest response a drug can produce, however much is given. Potency and efficacy are independent properties.

blocks.caption: E = response at drug concentration C; Emax = maximal response; EC50 = concentration giving half-maximal response. This hyperbolic equation follows from the law of mass action for simple receptor binding, assuming response is proportional to receptor occupancy.

blocks.title: Reading potency and efficacy from curve data
blocks.prompt: Drug X has Emax = 100 units and EC50 = 0.5 micromolar (uM). Drug Y has Emax = 100 units and EC50 = 5 uM. Compare potency and efficacy and calculate the response of drug X at 1.5 uM.

steps.text: Compare Emax: both are 100 units, so efficacy is equal.
Compare EC50: X is 0.5 uM and Y is 5 uM. X needs ten times less drug for half-maximal effect, so X is ten times more potent.
Calculate the response of X at 1.5 uM.
Interpret: on the same plot, X's curve lies to the left of Y's but both curves flatten at the same height.

blocks.answer: X is ten-fold more potent, equally efficacious, and gives 75 units at 1.5 uM

blocks.caption: Potency compared with efficacy.
rows: Position left or right along the dose axis
Small dose gives the effect (low EC50)
A larger maximum response is possible
Determines the size of the dose (milligrams)
Determines what the drug can achieve at all
Bumetanide acts at a much lower dose than furosemide
Loop diuretics produce a greater maximum diuresis than thiazides

blocks.markdown: **Comparing drugs.** If one drug's curve is shifted to the left of another's but both reach the same plateau, the first is more potent but not more efficacious. If one curve plateaus lower, that drug has a lower efficacy and cannot match the other however much is given. Partial agonists show lower efficacy than full agonists even if they bind with high affinity. Clinically, **efficacy usually matters more than potency**: a drug that cannot produce the needed effect is of no use at any dose, whereas a less potent drug just needs a larger tablet, which matters little unless the dose becomes impractical or side effects rise.

blocks.title: Choosing between two drugs
blocks.prompt: Drug A has EC50 = 2 mg/L and Emax = 60 mmHg fall in blood pressure. Drug B has EC50 = 20 mg/L and Emax = 90 mmHg fall. The patient needs a 70 mmHg fall. Which drug can achieve it?

steps.text: Compare potency: A (2 mg/L) is ten times more potent than B (20 mg/L).
Compare efficacy: A cannot exceed a 60 mmHg fall; B can reach 90 mmHg.
The target is 70 mmHg, above A's ceiling, so no dose of A will achieve it. B can, at a sufficient concentration.
Check B's required concentration: 70 = 90 x C / (20 + C), so 70 x (20 + C) = 90C, so 1400 = 20C and C = 70 mg/L.

blocks.answer: Only drug B can achieve a 70 mmHg fall (needs about 70 mg/L); A is more potent but has lower efficacy.

blocks.title: The logarithmic dose axis
blocks.text: Dose-response curves are normally plotted against the logarithm of the dose. On a linear axis the curve is a hyperbola that is crowded at low doses. On a log axis it becomes a symmetrical sigmoid with a steep, nearly straight middle section.

items: It allows doses spanning several orders of magnitude (for example 0.01 to 100 mg) to be shown on one graph.
The central portion of the curve (about 20% to 80% of Emax) is approximately linear, making EC50 easy to read and compare.
Drugs acting at the same receptor give parallel curves, so a competitive antagonist shifts the curve to the right without changing its shape or height.
Equal distances on the axis represent equal ratios of dose (for example 10-fold), which reflects how biological responses scale.

blocks.title: Potency is not safety
blocks.text: A more potent drug is not necessarily more effective or safer. Potency only tells you the dose; clinical value depends on efficacy, adverse effects and selectivity.

points: EC50 measures potency (lower EC50 means higher potency); Emax measures efficacy (the maximum response).
Potency and efficacy are independent: curves differ in position along the dose axis, or in plateau height, or both.
A log dose axis turns the hyperbolic curve into a sigmoid, accommodates a wide dose range and makes comparison and antagonism easier to read.

questions.stem: What does the EC50 of a drug represent?

options.text: The concentration producing 50% of that drug's maximal response
The concentration producing a response in 50% of the population
The maximum response the drug can produce
The concentration at which half the drug has been eliminated

questions.correctOptionText: The concentration producing 50% of that drug's maximal response

distractorRationale.a: Correct: EC50 is the half-maximal effective concentration.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: that describes a quantal measure such as ED50 in a population.

questions.explanation: EC50 is read at the half-maximal point of a graded dose-response curve and is the standard index of potency. A lower EC50 means less drug is needed.

questions.stem: A drug lowers blood pressure with Emax = 40 mmHg and EC50 = 2 mg/L. Using E = Emax x C / (EC50 + C), calculate the fall in blood pressure in mmHg at a concentration of 6 mg/L.
questions.explanation: E = 40 x 6 / (2 + 6) = 240 / 8 = 30 mmHg. This is 75% of Emax, consistent with the concentration being three times EC50.

questions.stem: Drug P has an EC50 of 8 nM and drug Q has an EC50 of 0.4 nM at the same receptor and both reach the same Emax. How many times more potent is drug Q than drug P?
questions.explanation: Potency ratio = EC50 of P / EC50 of Q = 8 / 0.4 = 20. Q is 20 times more potent, but because their Emax values match, it is not more efficacious.

questions.stem: Drug M has a low EC50 and a maximal effect of 40% of the tissue maximum. Drug N has a higher EC50 and a maximal effect of 100%. Which statement is correct?

options.text: M is more potent and N is more efficacious
M is more potent and more efficacious
N is more potent and M is more efficacious
Neither can be compared because they have different EC50 values

questions.correctOptionText: M is more potent and N is more efficacious

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lower EC50 means M is more potent; higher Emax means N is more efficacious.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: potency and efficacy are compared separately.

questions.explanation: Potency is about position on the dose axis (EC50) and efficacy is about plateau height (Emax). M's curve is further left but flatter, while N's curve is to the right but climbs higher.

questions.stem: A patient needs a 20 mmHg fall in blood pressure that drug S, even at maximal dose, cannot achieve (Emax 12 mmHg), whereas drug T (Emax 35 mmHg) can. S is far more potent than T. Which is the best conclusion?

options.text: T is more suitable because its efficacy exceeds the required effect
S is more suitable because it is more potent
Increasing the dose of S will eventually give 20 mmHg
S and T are equivalent because they act at the same receptor

questions.correctOptionText: T is more suitable because its efficacy exceeds the required effect

distractorRationale.a: Correct: only T can produce the needed effect.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: potency only affects the dose size.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: S plateaus at 12 mmHg regardless of dose.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: shared receptor does not mean equal efficacy.

questions.explanation: The plateau of S's curve is the ceiling of what it can do, so no dose will reach 20 mmHg. Efficacy is therefore the deciding property, and potency only influences dose size.

questions.stem: Why is a graded dose-response curve usually plotted against the logarithm of the dose?

options.text: It converts the hyperbola to a sigmoid, accommodates a wide dose range and makes the mid-portion nearly linear
It increases the maximal effect of the drug
It makes EC50 independent of the drug
It removes the need to know the dose

questions.correctOptionText: It converts the hyperbola to a sigmoid, accommodates a wide dose range and makes the mid-portion nearly linear

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these are the practical advantages of a log axis.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: plotting does not change the drug's effect.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: EC50 is a property of the drug and system.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: the dose is still needed.

questions.explanation: A log scale spreads out the crowded low-dose region and compresses high doses, so a single graph can show several orders of magnitude. The sigmoid's linear middle section makes EC50 easy to identify and curves easy to compare.

questions.stem: A dose-response experiment tests doses from 0.01 mg to 100 mg in successive 10-fold steps. How many log10 units does the dose axis span?
questions.explanation: log10(100) - log10(0.01) = 2 - (-2) = 4. The range covers a 10,000-fold span, which would be impossible to display legibly on a linear axis.

questions.stem: Differentiate potency from efficacy, and explain why two drugs can differ in one without differing in the other.
markingGuide: Potency: dose or concentration needed for a given effect; indexed by EC50; lower EC50 = more potent
Efficacy: maximal response a drug can produce; indexed by Emax
Potency is the horizontal position of the curve, efficacy is its height
Drugs can differ in potency alone (parallel curves with same plateau) or efficacy alone (same EC50, different plateau)
Clinical point: efficacy usually matters more; potency mainly sets the dose size
questions.explanation: The two properties describe different features of the curve and arise from different drug characteristics, such as affinity and intrinsic activity. A drug can therefore be strong in one and weak in the other.

questions.stem: Explain the advantages of plotting a dose-response curve against log dose and describe the shape that results.
markingGuide: Linear plot gives a hyperbola with most change at low doses
Log plot gives a symmetrical sigmoid curve
Wide dose range (several orders of magnitude) can be shown on one axis
Middle section (approx. 20-80% of Emax) is nearly linear, so EC50 is easy to read
Parallel shifts allow comparison of potency or the effect of a competitive antagonist
questions.explanation: The log transformation gives a stable, symmetrical shape and spreads out the data. This makes it easier to read EC50 and to see parallel shifts between drugs.

questions.stem: True or false: a drug with a lower EC50 than another is always the better clinical choice.
questions.explanation: A lower EC50 only means the drug is more potent, so a smaller dose is needed. The better clinical choice depends on efficacy, adverse effects and other factors, not potency alone.
